column5: Adam’s expulsion and toil
column6: The commentary links Adam’s expulsion from the garden with hardship; Genesis makes the ground cursed and toil the consequence of his disobedience in the same story.

column5: bread by sweat
column6: The commentary recalls hardship following Adam’s exile; Genesis specifies that he eats bread by the sweat of his face, giving that hardship its daily labor.

column5: Terah served other gods
column6: The commentary’s Abraham asks to be kept from idol worship; Joshua says Abraham’s father and ancestors served other gods, locating the danger his prayer names.

column5: God took Abraham across the river
column6: The commentary has Abraham ask God to keep his family from idols; Joshua recounts God taking Abraham from beyond the Euphrates into Canaan, a narrated removal from his idolatrous setting.

column5: not in haste or flight; God goes before
column6: The commentary defines the guide as one who precedes and describes a calm walk rather than a flight; Isaiah joins both details, saying the departing people need not hurry or flee because God goes before them and guards their rear.

column5: hind-like feet on high places
column6: The commentary’s mountain ridge is long yet easier to climb and its mount has light legs; the psalm combines hind-like feet with being set on high places, an image of sure-footed ascent.

column5: righteous walk the same paths transgressors fall on
column6: The commentary says the road may be the same while the traveler’s manner differs; Hosea says the just walk in the Lord’s right ways while transgressors fall in those very ways.

column5: God teaches the way one should walk
column6: The commentary develops guidance as someone going ahead to show a road; the psalm has God instruct and teach the way the addressee should walk, making the guide’s instruction explicit.

column5: Wisdom’s counsel refused
column6: The commentary says the wretched person keeps the reminder at a distance; personified Wisdom says her hearers rejected her counsel and reproof, a concrete scene of refusing admonition.

column5: donkey turns aside from the blocked road
column6: The commentary’s mount is easy to lead and quick to follow; Balaam’s donkey instead leaves the road when it sees the angel blocking the way, and that refusal protects its rider.

column5: Balaam’s way is perverse
column6: The commentary makes the traveler’s conduct, not the road itself, decisive; the angel tells Balaam that his way is perverse, while the donkey’s apparent deviation is the safer response to the blocked path.

column5: two gates and roads with different ends
column6: The commentary sets a shown route beside a steep climb that is not attempted; Jesus describes a broad road entered by a wide gate that leads to destruction, making the traveler’s chosen way consequential.

column5: narrow way leading to life
column6: The commentary’s two high routes and the unattempted ascent invite comparison with Jesus’ narrow way to life, which few find; this adds a sharply difficult route alongside the easy-way image.

column5: one side of the afterlife sees the other
column6: In the commentary’s cited scene a person in bliss looks down and sees his former companion in Hell; Luke has the tormented rich man lift his eyes and see Lazarus with Abraham at a distance, reversing the direction of the postmortem gaze.

column5: horse or mule needs bit and bridle
column6: The commentary’s animal is pliant and follows readily; the psalm warns against an uncomprehending horse or mule that must be controlled with bit and bridle, a pointed contrast between willing guidance and restraint.

column5: wicked like windblown chaff
column6: The commentary’s verse turns pasture into debris; Psalm 1 uses chaff for the wicked, adding an ethical judgment to the image of vegetation reduced to residue.

column5: the wicked way perishes
column6: The commentary distinguishes the person who follows guidance from the one who avoids it; Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked that perishes, giving the two responses different ends.

column5: a highway on which even a fool will not stray
column6: The commentary describes being made ready for the easier way; Isaiah’s holy highway is so clearly marked that even a fool will not err on it, a concrete image of an accessible route.

column5: the command is not too hard or far away
column6: The commentary reads the promised easy way as a facilitated course; Deuteronomy says the command is not too difficult or remote, linking divine instruction with practicable action.

column5: choose life or death
column6: The commentary pairs guidance with the traveler’s response and outcome; Moses sets life and death before Israel and tells them to choose life, a direct choice between destinations.

column5: the word is near and doable
column6: The commentary’s easy way is prepared for its addressee; Deuteronomy places the word in mouth and heart, near enough to do, making accessibility an inward as well as traveled route.

column5: the shepherd leads in paths of righteousness
column6: The commentary pictures a guide leading the way; the psalm’s shepherd restores the speaker and leads him in righteous paths, joining care for the traveler to a directed route.

column5: a voice behind says, “This is the way”
column6: The commentary calls the guide one who goes ahead; Isaiah’s traveler hears a voice behind identifying the way to walk, a concrete reversal of the guide’s position while preserving the path instruction.

column5: one lifts a fallen companion
column6: The commentary’s lexical note describes a weak person walking while leaning on two others; Ecclesiastes says one companion raises another who falls, a close support image though not a description of walking gait.

column5: walk without growing faint
column6: The commentary brings together weakness, light legs, and easy travel; Isaiah says those who wait for the Lord walk without fainting, portraying renewed capacity for the journey.

column5: riding camels and following the guide
column6: The commentary’s easy-to-follow animal carries a rider along a route; Rebekah and her attendants ride camels and follow Abraham’s servant, a concrete guided journey on mounts.

column5: Rachel sits on the camel saddle
column6: The commentary describes a wrapped cover placed over a camel’s hump and then ridden; Genesis has Rachel sit on the camel’s saddle, supplying a biblical riding-seat scene, though it uses the saddle to conceal idols.

column5: Jacob tells his household to put away foreign gods
column6: The commentary contrasts keeping counsel away with Abraham asking God to keep him and his sons away from idols; Jacob directs his household to remove its foreign gods and purify itself, a family-level act of separation.

column5: foreign gods buried beneath the oak
column6: The commentary’s Abraham asks for protection from idol worship; Jacob’s household hands over its foreign gods, which Jacob buries beneath the oak, showing the concrete removal that follows his command.

column5: Abraham breaks his father’s idols
column6: The commentary recalls Abraham’s prayer that he and his descendants be kept from idol worship; Genesis Rabbah’s story of the young Abraham breaking the idols in Terah’s shop interprets that separation as an active rejection of his father’s cult.

column5: weary and burdened people receive rest
column6: The commentary reads the promise of ease as relief on a journey; Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him and promises rest, giving the ease image a human burden-bearing context.

column5: easy yoke and light burden
column6: The commentary’s mount is readily led and takes the way with light steps; Jesus calls his yoke easy and his burden light, applying ease to the discipline of following him.

column5: God promises to be with Moses’ mouth
column6: The commentary cites Moses asking God to make his task easy; when Moses objects to speaking, God promises to be with his mouth and teach him what to say, a narrative answer that equips him for the mission.

column5: possible Arabic s-w-y / Hebrew שוה cognate
column6: The commentary reports an Arabic family sense of equality alongside “middle”; Isaiah uses the Hebrew root שוה for being equal or compared. The semantic link is specific, but the cognate relationship needs lexical confirmation and does not carry the camel-seat sense.
